```{r}
#| label: setup

library(ggplot2)
library(here)

core <- utils::read.csv(
  here("simulation-atlas/data/atlas-summary.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE
)

diagnostic <- utils::read.csv(
  here("simulation-atlas/data/diagnostic-atlas-summary.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE
)

grid <- utils::read.csv(
  here("simulation-atlas/data/scenario-grid.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE
)

pct <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  ifelse(
    is.finite(x),
    paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = digits), "%"),
    "--"
  )
}

num <- function(x, digits = 3) {
  ifelse(is.finite(x), formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits), "--")
}

ci_text <- function(low, high, digits = 1) {
  paste0("[", pct(low, digits), ", ", pct(high, digits), "]")
}

# Slice identifiers are code-level values that use underscores. Underscores are
# unbreakable in the PDF tables, so display them with spaces instead.
slice_display <- function(x) gsub("_", " ", x, fixed = TRUE)

has_slice <- function(x, slice) {
  vapply(
    strsplit(ifelse(is.na(x), "", x), ";", fixed = TRUE),
    function(z) slice %in% z,
    logical(1)
  )
}

family_title <- c(
  forced_choice = "Simulation 1: Forced-choice accuracy and the non-zero chance floor",
  within_family = "Simulation 2: Within-family link choice, logit versus probit",
  sum_scores = "Simulation 3: Sum scores"
)

family_short <- c(
  forced_choice = "Forced-choice accuracy",
  within_family = "Logit vs probit",
  sum_scores = "Sum scores"
)

model_order <- list(
  forced_choice = c(
    "Chance-corrected binomial logit",
    "Standard binomial logit",
    "Standard binomial probit",
    "Gaussian identity"
  ),
  within_family = c("Binomial logit", "Binomial probit"),
  sum_scores = c(
    "Latent generating scale",
    "Gaussian-probit bounded score",
    "Observed sum-score identity"
  )
)

slice_specs <- list(
  forced_choice = data.frame(
    slice = c("sample_size", "scale_location", "trial_count", "chance_level"),
    label = c(
      "Sample size",
      "Intercept",
      "Trials per participant",
      "Chance level"
    ),
    variable = c("N", "beta_intercept", "k_trials", "chance"),
    xlab = c(
      "N",
      "Generating intercept",
      "Trials per participant",
      "Chance level"
    ),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ),
  within_family = data.frame(
    slice = c("sample_size", "trial_count", "latent_location", "icc"),
    label = c("Sample size", "Trials per cell", "Intercept", "Latent ICC"),
    variable = c(
      "n_subjects",
      "k_trials",
      "reference_beta_intercept",
      "target_icc"
    ),
    xlab = c(
      "Participants",
      "Trials per participant-condition cell",
      "Reference intercept",
      "Latent ICC"
    ),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ),
  sum_scores = data.frame(
    slice = c(
      "sample_size",
      "scale_location",
      "item_count",
      "latent_dispersion"
    ),
    label = c(
      "Sample size",
      "Scale location",
      "Number of items",
      "Latent dispersion"
    ),
    variable = c("N", "threshold_shift", "J", "theta_sd"),
    xlab = c("N", "Item-threshold shift", "Number of items", "Latent SD"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
)

family_rows <- function(family) {
  out <- core[core$family == family, , drop = FALSE]
  out$model_label <- factor(out$model_label, levels = model_order[[family]])
  out
}

anchor_rows <- function(family) {
  out <- family_rows(family)
  out[out$paper_anchor %in% TRUE, , drop = FALSE]
}

slice_rows <- function(family) {
  specs <- slice_specs[[family]]
  dat <- family_rows(family)
  pieces <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(specs)), function(i) {
    spec <- specs[i, ]
    keep <- has_slice(dat$slice_membership, spec$slice)
    out <- dat[keep, , drop = FALSE]
    out$slice_view <- spec$slice
    out$slice_label <- spec$label
    out$x_value <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(out[[spec$variable]]))
    out$x_label <- spec$xlab
    out
  })
  do.call(rbind, pieces)
}

surface_rows <- function(family) {
  dat <- family_rows(family)
  dat[has_slice(dat$slice_membership, "main_effect_surface"), , drop = FALSE]
}

anchor_table <- function(family) {
  dat <- anchor_rows(family)
  out <- data.frame(
    Scenario = dat$scenario_label,
    `Generating link/scale` = dat$generating_link,
    `Fitted model/scale` = as.character(dat$model_label),
    `Rate type` = dat$rate_type,
    `Rejection rate` = pct(dat$rejection_rate_ok),
    `95% CI` = ci_text(dat$rejection_ci_low_ok, dat$rejection_ci_high_ok),
    `Deterministic pseudo-interaction` = num(
      dat$deterministic_pseudo_interaction
    ),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
  if (family == "forced_choice") {
    out <- cbind(
      out,
      `Flagged fits` = dat$n_fit_problem,
      `Fit-problem rate` = pct(dat$fit_problem_rate),
      `Apparent rejection rate among flagged fits` = pct(
        dat$rejection_rate_problem
      )
    )
  }
  rownames(out) <- NULL
  out
}

plot_anchor_rates <- function(family) {
  dat <- anchor_rows(family)
  dat$model_label <- factor(dat$model_label, levels = model_order[[family]])

  ggplot(
    dat,
    aes(
      x = model_label,
      y = rejection_rate_ok,
      ymin = rejection_ci_low_ok,
      ymax = rejection_ci_high_ok,
      group = scenario_label,
      shape = scenario_label
    )
  ) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_pointrange(position = position_dodge(width = 0.55)) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      limits = c(0, 1),
      breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2),
      labels = function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")
    ) +
    labs(
      x = NULL,
      y = "Product-term rejection rate",
      shape = "Scenario"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1),
      legend.position = "top"
    )
}

plot_slice_rates <- function(family) {
  dat <- slice_rows(family)
  dat$model_label <- factor(dat$model_label, levels = model_order[[family]])
  dat$slice_label <- factor(
    dat$slice_label,
    levels = slice_specs[[family]]$label
  )

  p <- ggplot(
    dat,
    aes(
      x = x_value,
      y = rejection_rate_ok,
      group = model_label,
      linetype = model_label,
      shape = model_label
    )
  ) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.35) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      limits = c(0, 1),
      breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2),
      labels = function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")
    ) +
    labs(
      x = NULL,
      y = "Product-term rejection rate",
      linetype = "Fitted model",
      shape = "Fitted model"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      legend.position = "top"
    )

  if (family == "within_family") {
    p + facet_grid(generating_link ~ slice_label, scales = "free_x")
  } else {
    p + facet_wrap(~slice_label, scales = "free_x", ncol = 2)
  }
}

slice_range_table <- function(family) {
  dat <- slice_rows(family)
  key <- interaction(
    dat$slice_label,
    dat$generating_link,
    dat$model_label,
    drop = TRUE
  )
  split_dat <- split(dat, key)

  rows <- lapply(split_dat, function(x) {
    data.frame(
      Slice = x$slice_label[1],
      `Generating link/scale` = x$generating_link[1],
      `Fitted model/scale` = as.character(x$model_label[1]),
      `Minimum rejection rate` = pct(min(x$rejection_rate_ok, na.rm = TRUE)),
      `Maximum rejection rate` = pct(max(x$rejection_rate_ok, na.rm = TRUE)),
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  })

  out <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  rownames(out) <- NULL
  out
}

coefficient_values_text <- function(
  family,
  variable,
  generating_link = NULL,
  digits = 3
) {
  dat <- surface_rows(family)
  if (!is.null(generating_link)) {
    dat <- dat[dat$generating_link == generating_link, , drop = FALSE]
  }
  values <- sort(unique(dat[[variable]][is.finite(dat[[variable]])]))
  paste(formatC(values, format = "f", digits = digits), collapse = ", ")
}

plot_surface <- function(family) {
  dat <- surface_rows(family)
  dat$model_label <- factor(dat$model_label, levels = model_order[[family]])

  if (family == "forced_choice") {
    dat$surface_x <- factor(dat$beta_age, levels = sort(unique(dat$beta_age)))
    dat$surface_y <- factor(
      dat$beta_group,
      levels = sort(unique(dat$beta_group))
    )
    xlab <- "Age coefficient on generating scale"
    ylab <- "Group coefficient on generating scale"
  } else if (family == "within_family") {
    dat$surface_x <- factor(
      dat$beta_group,
      levels = sort(unique(dat$beta_group))
    )
    dat$surface_y <- factor(
      dat$beta_condition,
      levels = sort(unique(dat$beta_condition))
    )
    xlab <- "Group coefficient on generating link scale"
    ylab <- "Condition coefficient on generating link scale"
  } else {
    dat$surface_x <- factor(dat$beta_x, levels = sort(unique(dat$beta_x)))
    dat$surface_y <- factor(
      dat$beta_group,
      levels = sort(unique(dat$beta_group))
    )
    xlab <- "Predictor coefficient on latent generating scale"
    ylab <- "Group coefficient on latent generating scale"
  }

  p <- ggplot(
    dat,
    aes(
      x = surface_x,
      y = surface_y,
      fill = rejection_rate_ok
    )
  ) +
    geom_tile() +
    geom_text(
      aes(label = paste0(round(100 * rejection_rate_ok), "%")),
      size = 3,
      colour = "white"
    ) +
    scale_fill_gradient(
      limits = c(0, 1),
      breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.25),
      labels = function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")
    ) +
    labs(
      x = xlab,
      y = ylab,
      fill = "Rejection rate"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "right")

  if (family == "within_family") {
    p +
      facet_wrap(vars(generating_link, model_label), ncol = 2, scales = "free")
  } else {
    p + facet_wrap(~model_label)
  }
}

rate_range <- function(family, model = NULL, rate_type = NULL) {
  dat <- family_rows(family)
  if (!is.null(model)) {
    dat <- dat[as.character(dat$model_label) == model, , drop = FALSE]
  }
  if (!is.null(rate_type)) {
    dat <- dat[dat$rate_type == rate_type, , drop = FALSE]
  }
  range(dat$rejection_rate_ok, na.rm = TRUE)
}

rate_range_text <- function(...) {
  r <- rate_range(...)
  paste0(pct(r[1]), " to ", pct(r[2]))
}

# Compact scenario-level appendix. Keep only columns needed to reconstruct the
# scientific result without reproducing the wide machine-readable CSV.
compact_core_table <- function(family) {
  dat <- family_rows(family)
  out <- data.frame(
    ID = dat$scenario_id,
    Slice = slice_display(dat$slice),
    Scenario = dat$scenario_label,
    `Generating link/scale` = dat$generating_link,
    `Fitted model/scale` = as.character(dat$model_label),
    `Rejection rate` = pct(dat$rejection_rate_ok),
    `Deterministic pseudo-interaction` = num(
      dat$deterministic_pseudo_interaction
    ),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
  if (family == "forced_choice") {
    out <- cbind(
      out,
      `Fit-problem rate` = pct(dat$fit_problem_rate),
      `Apparent rejection rate among flagged fits` = pct(
        dat$rejection_rate_problem
      )
    )
  }
  rownames(out) <- NULL
  out
}

  } else {

# Diagnostic helpers -------------------------------------------------------

# Diagnostic cases in the order of the manuscript diagnostic table
diagnostic_family_title <- c(
  count = "Poisson count: log generated, identity fitted",
  forced_choice = "Forced-choice chance-floor case",
  within_family = "Probit-generated, logit-fitted case",
  binary_continuous = "Binary continuous predictor: probit generated, logit fitted",
  gamma = "Gamma: log generated, inverse fitted"
)
diagnostic_families <- names(diagnostic_family_title)

# Sample size is N, or the number of subjects for the repeated-trial binary cases.
# Severity is the intercept (reference intercept for the binary cases), or a common
# multiplier of the two main effects for the count and Gamma cases.
diagnostic_n_column <- c(
  count = "N",
  forced_choice = "N",
  within_family = "n_subjects",
  binary_continuous = "n_subjects",
  gamma = "N"
)
diagnostic_severity_column <- c(
  count = "beta_main_1_multiplier",
  forced_choice = "beta_intercept",
  within_family = "reference_beta_intercept",
  binary_continuous = "reference_beta_intercept",
  gamma = "beta_main_1_multiplier"
)
diagnostic_severity_label <- c(
  count = "Main-effect multiplier",
  forced_choice = "Intercept",
  within_family = "Intercept",
  binary_continuous = "Intercept",
  gamma = "Main-effect multiplier"
)

# Values quoted in the diagnostic text
dg_rate <- function(id, check = "AIC favors generating link", column = "detection_rate") {
  diagnostic[diagnostic$scenario_id == id & diagnostic$diagnostic == check, column][1]
}
dg_rows <- function(families, pattern) {
  diagnostic[
    diagnostic$family %in% families &
      diagnostic$applicable %in% TRUE &
      diagnostic$computed %in% TRUE &
      grepl(pattern, diagnostic$diagnostic),
    ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]
}
dg_max <- function(families, pattern, column = "detection_rate") {
  max(dg_rows(families, pattern)[[column]], na.rm = TRUE)
}
dg_min <- function(families, pattern, column = "detection_rate") {
  min(dg_rows(families, pattern)[[column]], na.rm = TRUE)
}
binomial_cases <- c("forced_choice", "within_family", "binary_continuous")
# largest excess of wrong-link over correct-link DHARMa flagging, in percentage points
dharma_excess_binomial <- with(
  dg_rows(binomial_cases, "^DHARMa"),
  max(detection_rate - correct_link_flag_rate, na.rm = TRUE)
)
pseudo_max_fc <- max(
  diagnostic$pseudo_interaction_detection_rate[diagnostic$family == "forced_choice"],
  na.rm = TRUE
)

diagnostic_expand_slices <- function(dat) {
  pieces <- list()
  counter <- 1L

  for (slice in c("sample_size", "severity")) {
    keep <- has_slice(dat$diagnostic_slice_membership, slice)
    out <- dat[keep, , drop = FALSE]
    if (!nrow(out)) {
      next
    }

    out$slice_view <- slice
    out$slice_label <- if (slice == "sample_size") {
      rep("Sample size", nrow(out))
    } else {
      unname(diagnostic_severity_label[out$family])
    }
    out$x_value <- NA_real_
    columns <- if (slice == "sample_size") {
      diagnostic_n_column
    } else {
      diagnostic_severity_column
    }
    for (r in seq_len(nrow(out))) {
      out$x_value[r] <- out[[columns[[out$family[r]]]]][r]
    }

    pieces[[counter]] <- out
    counter <- counter + 1L
  }

  out <- do.call(rbind, pieces)
  # case, then slice, then setting; order() keeps the original order of ties
  out[order(
    match(out$family, diagnostic_families),
    match(out$slice_view, c("sample_size", "severity")),
    out$x_value
  ), , drop = FALSE]
}

# One row per scenario, slice and plotted quantity. DHARMa is summarized by the
# highest flagging rate across the applicable residual checks, as the upper end
# of the DHARMa range in the manuscript diagnostic table; the separate checks
# are reported in the calibration table of the appendix.
make_diagnostic_plot_data <- function() {
  base <- diagnostic[
    diagnostic$family %in% diagnostic_families &
      diagnostic$applicable %in% TRUE &
      diagnostic$computed %in% TRUE,
    ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]
  dat <- diagnostic_expand_slices(base)
  # one panel per case and slice, in the order of diagnostic_expand_slices();
  # the manuscript anchor belongs to both slices and is shown in both
  dat$panel <- paste0(
    unname(diagnostic_family_title[dat$family]),
    "\n",
    dat$slice_label
  )
  panel_levels <- unique(dat$panel)
  max_or_na <- function(x) if (any(is.finite(x))) max(x[is.finite(x)]) else NA_real_

  key <- paste(dat$scenario_id, dat$panel)
  out <- NULL
  for (k in unique(key)) {
    x <- dat[key == k, , drop = FALSE]
    dh <- x[startsWith(x$diagnostic, "DHARMa"), , drop = FALSE]
    pg <- x[startsWith(x$diagnostic, "Pregibon"), , drop = FALSE]
    ai <- x[x$diagnostic == "AIC favors generating link", , drop = FALSE]
    out <- rbind(out, data.frame(
      panel = x$panel[1],
      x_value = x$x_value[1],
      quantity = c(
        "Pseudo-interaction detection",
        "AIC favors generating link",
        "DHARMa, highest check",
        "Pregibon-style check",
        "DHARMa, highest check",
        "Pregibon-style check"
      ),
      model = c(
        "Wrong link",
        "Wrong link",
        "Wrong link",
        "Wrong link",
        "Correct link",
        "Correct link"
      ),
      rate = c(
        x$pseudo_interaction_detection_rate[1],
        if (nrow(ai)) ai$detection_rate[1] else NA_real_,
        max_or_na(dh$detection_rate),
        if (nrow(pg)) pg$detection_rate[1] else NA_real_,
        max_or_na(dh$correct_link_flag_rate),
        if (nrow(pg)) pg$correct_link_flag_rate[1] else NA_real_
      )
    ))
  }
  out <- out[is.finite(out$rate), , drop = FALSE]
  out$panel <- factor(out$panel, levels = panel_levels)
  out
}

diagnostic_plot_theme <- function(p) {
  p +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      limits = c(0, 1),
      breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2),
      labels = function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")
    ) +
    # facet_wrap, not facet_grid, so that each panel has its own x scale
    # (the severity setting is an intercept or a main-effect multiplier)
    facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 2, scales = "free_x") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "top")
}

# Wrong-link model: pseudo-interaction, AIC, and how often each check flags it
plot_diagnostic_atlas <- function() {
  dat <- make_diagnostic_plot_data()
  dat <- dat[dat$model == "Wrong link", , drop = FALSE]
  dat$quantity <- factor(dat$quantity, levels = c(
    "Pseudo-interaction detection",
    "AIC favors generating link",
    "Pregibon-style check",
    "DHARMa, highest check"
  ))

  p <- ggplot(
    dat,
    aes(
      x = x_value,
      y = rate,
      group = quantity,
      linetype = quantity,
      shape = quantity
    )
  ) +
    labs(
      x = NULL,
      y = "Detection / selection rate",
      linetype = NULL,
      shape = NULL
    )
  diagnostic_plot_theme(p)
}

# The same checks on the wrong-link and on the correct-link model: a check is
# informative about the link only if the first rate clearly exceeds the second
plot_diagnostic_calibration <- function() {
  dat <- make_diagnostic_plot_data()
  dat <- dat[dat$quantity %in% c("DHARMa, highest check", "Pregibon-style check"), , drop = FALSE]
  dat$model <- factor(dat$model, levels = c("Wrong link", "Correct link"))
  dat$series <- interaction(dat$quantity, dat$model, sep = ", ", drop = TRUE)

  p <- ggplot(
    dat,
    aes(
      x = x_value,
      y = rate,
      group = series,
      linetype = model,
      shape = quantity
    )
  ) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.35) +
    labs(
      x = NULL,
      y = "Flagging rate",
      linetype = NULL,
      shape = NULL
    )
  diagnostic_plot_theme(p)
}

aic_table <- function() {
  base <- diagnostic[
    diagnostic$family %in%
      diagnostic_families &
      diagnostic$diagnostic == "AIC favors generating link",
    ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]
  dat <- diagnostic_expand_slices(base)

  setting_value <- ifelse(
    dat$slice_label == "Sample size",
    formatC(dat$x_value, format = "f", digits = 0),
    formatC(dat$x_value, format = "f", digits = 2)
  )

  out <- data.frame(
    Case = unname(diagnostic_family_title[dat$family]),
    Setting = paste0(dat$slice_label, " = ", setting_value),
    # share of replications with a finite product-term test under the wrong link
    `Wrong-link fits` = pct(dat$pseudo_interaction_n_successful / dat$n_attempted),
    `Pseudo-interaction detection` = pct(dat$pseudo_interaction_detection_rate),
    `AIC favors generating link` = pct(dat$detection_rate),
    `Median delta AIC` = num(dat$aic_delta_median, 2),
    `Delta AIC IQR` = paste0(
      "[",
      num(dat$aic_delta_q25, 2),
      ", ",
      num(dat$aic_delta_q75, 2),
      "]"
    ),
    `Absolute delta AIC < 2` = pct(dat$aic_delta_within_two_rate),
    check.names = FALSE
  )

  rownames(out) <- NULL
  out
}

diagnostic_used_table <- function() {
  dat <- diagnostic[
    diagnostic$family %in%
      diagnostic_families &
      diagnostic$applicable %in% TRUE &
      diagnostic$computed %in% TRUE,
    ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]
  parts <- split(dat, factor(dat$family, levels = diagnostic_families))
  parts <- parts[vapply(parts, nrow, integer(1)) > 0]
  out <- do.call(
    rbind,
    lapply(parts, function(x) {
      data.frame(
        `Diagnostic case` = unname(diagnostic_family_title[x$family[1]]),
        `Diagnostics used` = paste(unique(x$diagnostic), collapse = "; "),
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
        check.names = FALSE
      )
    })
  )
  rownames(out) <- NULL
  out
}

calibration_table <- function() {
  base <- diagnostic[
    diagnostic$family %in%
      diagnostic_families &
      diagnostic$applicable %in% TRUE &
      diagnostic$computed %in% TRUE &
      diagnostic$diagnostic != "AIC favors generating link",
    ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]
  dat <- diagnostic_expand_slices(base)

  setting_value <- ifelse(
    dat$slice_label == "Sample size",
    formatC(dat$x_value, format = "f", digits = 0),
    formatC(dat$x_value, format = "f", digits = 2)
  )

  out <- data.frame(
    Case = unname(diagnostic_family_title[dat$family]),
    Setting = paste0(dat$slice_label, " = ", setting_value),
    Diagnostic = dat$diagnostic,
    `Wrong-link flagging` = pct(dat$detection_rate),
    `Correct-link flagging` = pct(dat$correct_link_flag_rate),
    check.names = FALSE
  )

  rownames(out) <- NULL
  out
}

scenario_counts <- table(grid$family)
```

# Purpose and scope

Supplement B extends the three manuscript simulations and the diagnostic simulation by varying selected parameters while keeping the true interaction equal to zero on the generating scale. It uses one-dimensional sensitivity slices and small main-effect surfaces rather than a full Cartesian design.

Reference scenarios retain the generating settings of the corresponding manuscript simulations. In every scenario, a rejection under the matched generating model estimates the nominal generating-scale rejection rate; under another scale, it is a **pseudo-interaction detection rate**. For forced choice, these primary rates use finite tests from fits passing the minimal lme4 fit-quality checks. Apparent rejection rates among flagged fits are reported separately. For the logit-probit and sum-score families, as in the manuscript, the rates use every finite test. Publication runs request 3,000 Monte Carlo replications.

## How to read the figures

All rejection-rate figures use the same interpretation. The horizontal dashed line at .05 marks nominal alpha. Rates close to .05 under the generating scale provide a calibration check. Elevated rates under an alternative fitted scale show how often the scale difference becomes a statistically significant product term at the stated sample size and design. Error bars are shown for the reference scenarios. The sensitivity plots omit error bars to keep the larger set of scenarios readable; Wilson 95% intervals are available in the numerical tables and in `data/atlas-summary.csv`.

The deterministic pseudo-interaction reported in the tables is calculated from expected values before sampling. For forced choice and the other mixed-model family, it is evaluated at random intercept 0, not as a marginal population-average probability. It describes the interaction contrast implied by evaluating the generating pattern on the fitted scale. The Monte Carlo rejection rate adds sampling variability, standard errors, and sample size to that deterministic discrepancy.

# Atlas design

```{r}
#| label: tbl-atlas-design
#| tbl-cap: "Structure of the simulation atlas. Each family contains reference scenarios plus prespecified sensitivity slices."

design_table <- data.frame(
  `Manuscript case` = c(
    "Simulation 1: Forced-choice accuracy",
    "Simulation 2: Logit vs probit",
    "Simulation 3: Sum scores"
  ),
  `Generating scenarios` = c(
    scenario_counts[["forced_choice"]],
    scenario_counts[["within_family"]],
    scenario_counts[["sum_scores"]]
  ),
  `Sensitivity slices` = c(
    "Main effects; sample size; intercept; trials; chance level",
    "Main effects; sample size; trials; intercept; ICC",
    "Main effects; sample size; scale location; item count; latent dispersion"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(design_table, align = c("l", "r", "l"))
```

The one-dimensional slices change one named parameter while holding the remaining settings at the central reference scenario. The main-effect surfaces vary the two additive main-effect coefficients jointly. The actual coefficients are reported on the figure axes and in the table below.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-atlas-main-effect-coefficients
#| tbl-cap: "Generating-scale coefficients used in the main-effect surfaces. Coefficients are reported on the scale that generated each scenario."

knitr::kable(
  main_effect_coefficient_table(),
  align = c("l", "l", "l", "l", "l", "l")
)
```

For Simulation 2, logit and probit coefficients are on different generating-link scales. As in the manuscript simulation, the logit coefficients are scaled by 1.65 relative to the probit reference coefficients so that the two generating scenarios have similar cell probabilities. The figures therefore report the actual coefficient values for each generating link instead of a common relative index.


# Simulation 1: Forced-choice accuracy and the non-zero chance floor

Forced-choice accuracy is generated as trial-level Bernoulli responses from a chance-corrected binomial logit mixed model with a .50 floor, a subject random intercept, and no age-by-group product term on the conditional chance-corrected-logit scale. The subject random-intercept SD corresponds to latent-scale ICC $.30$ under the usual logistic convention. The fitted models are a matched chance-corrected-logit GLMM using `psyphy::mafc.logit` (with `nAGQ = 10`, as in the manuscript), standard binomial-logit and binomial-probit GLMMs, and a Gaussian identity LMM. All four use the same `(1 | id)` structure.

## Reference scenarios

```{r}
#| label: fig-atlas-fc-anchor
#| fig-cap: "Forced-choice reference scenarios. The product term is zero on the conditional chance-corrected-logit generating scale. Rates use fits passing the minimal fit-quality checks. The dashed line marks alpha = .05."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.8

plot_anchor_rates("forced_choice")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-atlas-fc-anchor
#| tbl-cap: "Forced-choice reference scenarios. The deterministic pseudo-interaction is evaluated on each fitted scale before sampling."

knitr::kable(
  anchor_table("forced_choice"),
  align = c("l", "l", "l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r")
)
```

Across the atlas, the matched chance-corrected-logit model rejects from `r rate_range_text("forced_choice", model = "Chance-corrected binomial logit")`. The standard binomial logit ranges from `r rate_range_text("forced_choice", model = "Standard binomial logit")`, the standard binomial probit from `r rate_range_text("forced_choice", model = "Standard binomial probit")`, and the Gaussian identity model from `r rate_range_text("forced_choice", model = "Gaussian identity")`. These rates use fits passing the minimal fit-quality checks; the share of flagged fits reaches `r pct(max(family_rows("forced_choice")$fit_problem_rate, na.rm = TRUE))` in some scenarios, and the appendix tables report it scenario by scenario. For the standard binomial GLMMs, the wrong-scale rates vary most with the size of the main effects and with sample size; the intercept, the number of trials and the chance level change them less within the declared ranges.

## One-dimensional sensitivity slices

```{r}
#| label: fig-atlas-fc-slices
#| fig-cap: "Forced-choice sensitivity slices. One parameter varies at a time around the central reference scenario. The dashed line marks alpha = .05."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

plot_slice_rates("forced_choice")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-atlas-fc-slice-ranges
#| tbl-cap: "Range of rejection rates across each forced-choice sensitivity slice."

knitr::kable(
  slice_range_table("forced_choice"),
  align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r")
)
```

The slices separate distinct reasons why a deterministic scale discrepancy may or may not become a statistical interaction. The intercept and the chance level change the curvature relevant to the fitted link. Sample size and number of trials change how precisely that discrepancy is estimated. The figure therefore distinguishes the existence of a pseudo-interaction on the fitted scale from the probability that a product-term test detects it.

## Main-effect surface

```{r}
#| label: fig-atlas-fc-surface
#| fig-cap: "Forced-choice main-effect surface. Axes report the age and group coefficients on the chance-corrected logit generating scale. Cell labels are product-term rejection rates."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.8

plot_surface("forced_choice")
```

The surface directly targets the mechanism emphasized in the manuscript. Two additive main effects can jointly move observations through regions where equal differences on the generating scale map to unequal differences on the fitted scale. Larger main effects can therefore increase the deterministic pseudo-interaction even though the generating age-by-group term remains zero.

# Simulation 2: Within-family link choice, logit versus probit

Repeated-trial random-intercept GLMMs cross logit and probit generating and fitted links. Both use the binomial family and the same 0-to-1 bounds, but impose additivity on different scales; the figures and Table 1 show the sensitivity design.

## Reference scenarios

```{r}
#| label: fig-atlas-wf-anchor
#| fig-cap: "Logit-probit reference scenarios. The product term is zero on the generating link scale. The dashed line marks alpha = .05."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.8

plot_anchor_rates("within_family")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-atlas-wf-anchor
#| tbl-cap: "Within-family reference scenarios for logit and probit generating links."

knitr::kable(
  anchor_table("within_family"),
  align = c("l", "l", "l", "l", "r", "r", "r")
)
```

Across the atlas, matched logit/probit fits remain near the nominal rejection rate. The wrong-link rows range from `r pct(min(family_rows("within_family")$rejection_rate_ok[family_rows("within_family")$rate_type == "Pseudo-interaction detection rate"], na.rm = TRUE))` to `r pct(max(family_rows("within_family")$rejection_rate_ok[family_rows("within_family")$rate_type == "Pseudo-interaction detection rate"], na.rm = TRUE))`. The range is wider than the reference scenarios alone suggest because the atlas deliberately varies information and the region of the latent scale. The result remains conditional on these declared slices and should not be read as a general frequency for logit-probit disagreement.

## One-dimensional sensitivity slices

```{r}
#| label: fig-atlas-wf-slices
#| fig-cap: "Logit-probit sensitivity slices. Rows identify the generating link. Within each panel the fitted logit and probit models are compared as one parameter varies around the reference scenario."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

plot_slice_rates("within_family")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-atlas-wf-slice-ranges
#| tbl-cap: "Range of rejection rates across each within-family sensitivity slice."

knitr::kable(
  slice_range_table("within_family"),
  align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r")
)
```

Sample size and trial count mainly change how detectable the small systematic discrepancy between the links becomes. The intercept and the main-effect magnitudes change the discrepancy itself by moving cell probabilities into regions where logit and probit curvature differs more. ICC changes the information structure of the repeated observations while leaving the fixed generating interaction at zero.

## Main-effect surface

```{r}
#| label: fig-atlas-wf-surface
#| fig-cap: "Within-family main-effect surfaces. Axes report the group and condition coefficients on each generating-link scale. Panels identify the generating and fitted links. Cell labels are product-term rejection rates."
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 6.5

plot_surface("within_family")
```

The matched-link panels provide the calibration reference. The off-diagonal panels show when the small difference between two standard binomial links becomes consequential for an interaction claim. This is the narrow point of the within-family example: logit and probit can remain very similar for prediction while defining sufficiently different additivity baselines to change a product-term conclusion under high information or strong curvature.

# Simulation 3: Sum scores

Sum-score data are generated on a latent continuous scale with no x-by-group interaction, converted to ordinal item responses, and summed. Analyses compare the latent generating scale, observed sum-score identity model, and Gaussian-probit bounded-score sensitivity model; the figures and Table 1 show the sensitivity design.

## Reference scenarios

```{r}
#| label: fig-atlas-ss-anchor
#| fig-cap: "Sum-score reference scenarios. The product term is zero on the latent generating scale. The dashed line marks alpha = .05."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.8

plot_anchor_rates("sum_scores")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-atlas-ss-anchor
#| tbl-cap: "Sum-score reference scenarios. The latent generating scale is available only in simulation."

knitr::kable(
  anchor_table("sum_scores"),
  align = c("l", "l", "l", "l", "r", "r", "r")
)
```

Across the atlas, the latent generating scale rejects from `r rate_range_text("sum_scores", model = "Latent generating scale")`. The observed sum-score identity model ranges from `r rate_range_text("sum_scores", model = "Observed sum-score identity")`, while the Gaussian-probit bounded-score sensitivity model ranges from `r rate_range_text("sum_scores", model = "Gaussian-probit bounded score")`. The latter remains a model of the manifest total. It does not recover the latent construct and should be read as a sensitivity analysis for the scale on which additivity is imposed.

## One-dimensional sensitivity slices

```{r}
#| label: fig-atlas-ss-slices
#| fig-cap: "Sum-score sensitivity slices. One parameter varies at a time around the central reference scenario. The dashed line marks alpha = .05."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

plot_slice_rates("sum_scores")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-atlas-ss-slice-ranges
#| tbl-cap: "Range of rejection rates across each sum-score sensitivity slice."

knitr::kable(
  slice_range_table("sum_scores"),
  align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r")
)
```

The scale-location slice changes how strongly the bounded sum score compresses the latent dimension. Item count and latent dispersion change the mapping between the latent variable and the manifest total. Sample size changes the probability that any resulting fitted-scale interaction is detected. These are distinct components of the sum-score problem and should not be reduced to a generic floor-or-ceiling warning.

## Main-effect surface

```{r}
#| label: fig-atlas-ss-surface
#| fig-cap: "Sum-score main-effect surface. Axes report the predictor and group coefficients on the latent generating scale. Cell labels are product-term rejection rates."
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 5.8

plot_surface("sum_scores")
```

The surface shows how the mapping from latent values to a bounded total can turn two additive latent effects into a non-additive pattern on the manifest score. The latent benchmark remains the calibration reference because its product term is zero by construction.

# Diagnostic atlas

The diagnostic analyses cover the five diagnostic scenarios of the manuscript, with the same data-generating processes and paired models: a Poisson count generated with a log link and fitted with an identity link; the forced-choice chance-floor case, with standard-logit and chance-corrected-logit GLMMs (`nAGQ = 10` for the chance-corrected GLMM); the probit-generated, logit-fitted repeated-trial case with a 2 x 2 design; its counterpart with a continuous predictor, x ~ Uniform(0, 1), and 30 trials per subject; and a Gamma response generated with a log link and fitted with an inverse link. For each case, the manuscript scenario is the reference, and the other scenarios vary sample size and severity one at a time. Severity is the intercept for the forced-choice and the two binary repeated-trial cases, where it moves the expected values along the curved part of the link. For the count and Gamma cases, it is a common multiplier of the two main effects, which sets how much curvature the two links show over the observed range: there the intercept only rescales the means, and with the inverse Gamma link it leaves the fitted model unchanged. The checks are those of the manuscript and Supplement A: DHARMa with its default settings, and the Pregibon-style added-term check refitted with the family, link, random intercept, and quadrature setting of the model being diagnosed.

Diagnostics are applied to the **misspecified interaction model**, matching the manuscript's post-estimation question: once the fitted model has produced the product-term finding, does that same model show enough evidence of misspecification to warn the analyst? As in the manuscript, the same DHARMa and Pregibon-style checks are also applied to the generating-link interaction model as a calibration reference (@tbl-atlas-diagnostic-calibration). AIC compares prespecified candidate mean models with the same structural interaction formula. Positive delta AIC, defined as AIC of the misspecified model minus AIC of the generating model, favors the generating link.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-atlas-diagnostic-status
#| tbl-cap: "Diagnostics used for each diagnostic case."

knitr::kable(diagnostic_used_table(), align = c("l", "l"))
```

Checks not listed were not applicable to the design. In particular, the design-cell residual check is used only for the 2 x 2 repeated-trial case, whereas residual quantile checks over a focal predictor require a continuous predictor (age for the count and forced-choice cases, x for the other two). The Pregibon-style check is not identifiable in the saturated 2 x 2 interaction model.

## Detection across sensitivity slices

```{r}
#| label: fig-atlas-diagnostics
#| fig-cap: "Diagnostic atlas, misspecified interaction model. Pseudo-interaction detection is shown together with the AIC comparison, the Pregibon-style check and the most sensitive DHARMa residual check of each scenario. For each case, the sample-size slice (left) and the severity slice (right; intercept, or multiplier of the two main effects) are shown separately; the manuscript scenario appears in both."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 15

plot_diagnostic_atlas()
```

The rates in this figure answer different questions. Pseudo-interaction detection is the probability that the misspecified fitted scale yields a significant product term. Pregibon-style detection is the probability that the added-term link check flags a departure. AIC reports how often the generating link has the lower AIC within the specified candidate pair. The curves therefore need not be complements of one another. Diagnostic misalignment occurs when the interaction conclusion changes more readily than the diagnostic workflow signals a problem. DHARMa is summarized by the highest flagging rate across its applicable residual checks, the upper end of the DHARMa range in the manuscript diagnostic table; the individual checks are reported in @tbl-atlas-diagnostic-calibration.

In the count and Gamma cases the checks followed the pseudo-interaction. Across their slices, the Pregibon-style check flagged the identity-link count model in `r pct(dg_min("count", "^Pregibon"))` to `r pct(dg_max("count", "^Pregibon"))` of replications and the inverse-link Gamma model in `r pct(dg_min("gamma", "^Pregibon"))` to `r pct(dg_max("gamma", "^Pregibon"))`, rising with sample size and main-effect size together with pseudo-interaction detection, while it flagged the correct-link models in at most `r pct(dg_max(c("count", "gamma"), "^Pregibon", "correct_link_flag_rate"))`. Among the residual checks, the quantile check over the focal predictor was the most sensitive. It flagged the count model almost always with larger samples or stronger main effects than in the manuscript scenario, but the Gamma model in at most `r pct(dg_max("gamma", "focal predictor"))` of replications, at the strongest main effects.

The three binomial cases differ. In no scenario did a DHARMa check flag the misspecified model more than `r formatC(100 * dharma_excess_binomial, format = "f", digits = 1)` percentage points more often than the correct-link model, although pseudo-interaction detection reached `r pct(pseudo_max_fc)` in the forced-choice case. The Pregibon-style check separated the two forced-choice models only in larger samples and at the highest intercept: at N = 1000 it flagged the standard logit in `r pct(dg_rate("D-FC-004", "Pregibon-style added-term link check"))` of replications and the chance-corrected logit in `r pct(dg_rate("D-FC-004", "Pregibon-style added-term link check", "correct_link_flag_rate"))`, and at intercept 1.50 in `r pct(dg_rate("D-FC-008", "Pregibon-style added-term link check"))` and `r pct(dg_rate("D-FC-008", "Pregibon-style added-term link check", "correct_link_flag_rate"))`, whereas at N = 100 and 250 it flagged the correct model more often, as in the manuscript. In the binary continuous-predictor case it flagged either model in `r pct(min(dg_min("binary_continuous", "^Pregibon"), dg_min("binary_continuous", "^Pregibon", "correct_link_flag_rate")))` to `r pct(max(dg_max("binary_continuous", "^Pregibon"), dg_max("binary_continuous", "^Pregibon", "correct_link_flag_rate")))` of replications in every scenario, close to the nominal rate.

## Calibration of the checks

```{r}
#| label: fig-atlas-diagnostic-calibration
#| fig-cap: "The same checks applied to the misspecified (solid) and to the correctly specified (dashed) interaction model fitted to the same data. A check is informative about the link only when the first rate clearly exceeds the second. DHARMa: highest flagging rate across the applicable residual checks, so the two DHARMa lines may refer to different checks. The dotted line marks nominal alpha."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 15

plot_diagnostic_calibration()
```

With the package defaults, DHARMa flagged the correctly specified mixed models more often as the number of participants grew. In the forced-choice case at N = 1000, the dispersion check flagged the correct chance-corrected model in `r pct(dg_rate("D-FC-004", "DHARMa dispersion", "correct_link_flag_rate"))` of replications and the uniformity check in `r pct(dg_rate("D-FC-004", "DHARMa uniformity", "correct_link_flag_rate"))`. With 1200 subjects, the design-cell check flagged the correct probit model in `r pct(dg_rate("D-WF-004", "DHARMa residual distribution across design cells", "correct_link_flag_rate"))` of replications in the 2 x 2 case, and the quantile check over fitted values did so in `r pct(dg_rate("D-BC-004", "DHARMa residual quantiles over fitted values", "correct_link_flag_rate"))` in the continuous-predictor case. In these cases, a larger sample made the residual checks fire more often under both links instead of separating them. For the count and Gamma GLMs, correct-link flagging stayed at or below `r pct(dg_max(c("count", "gamma"), "^DHARMa", "correct_link_flag_rate"))`, the highest value occurring in the smallest count sample.

## Strength of the AIC comparison

```{r}
#| label: tbl-atlas-aic
#| tbl-cap: "AIC comparison across the diagnostic atlas. Positive delta AIC favors the generating link. The within-two column reports the proportion of finite comparisons with absolute delta AIC below 2."

report_kable(aic_table(), align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"), long = TRUE)
```

The AIC win rate is reported together with the magnitude of the difference because these describe different situations. A generating link that wins frequently by a very small margin is weaker evidence than one that wins by a large margin. As in the manuscript, these comparisons rank a limited candidate set. They do not identify the substantively correct scale by themselves.

AIC favored the generating link in at least `r pct(dg_min(binomial_cases, "^AIC"))` of replications in every binomial scenario and in at least `r pct(dg_min("count", "^AIC"))` in the count scenarios. In the Gamma case it did so in `r pct(dg_min("gamma", "^AIC"))` to `r pct(dg_max("gamma", "^AIC"))` of replications, and with the main effects halved the absolute difference was below 2 in `r pct(dg_rate("D-GA-005", column = "aic_delta_within_two_rate"))` of them.

The wrong-link fits column reports how often the misspecified model returned a finite product-term test. In the count case the identity-link Poisson fit, which needs positive fitted means, often failed when the main effects were large: it returned a test in `r pct(dg_rate("D-CT-007", column = "fit_success_rate"))` of replications at multiplier 1.25 and in `r pct(dg_rate("D-CT-008", column = "fit_success_rate"))` at 1.5. All rates for these two scenarios are conditional on the successful fits; as in the manuscript, non-converged GLMs are treated as failed fits.

# Scope and interpretation

The sensitivity results show whether the reference scenarios reflect broader patterns or depend on a narrow configuration. They also distinguish parameters that change the **deterministic scale discrepancy**, such as the intercept and main-effect magnitude, from parameters that mainly change **detectability**, such as sample size and trial count. The diagnostic analyses place pseudo-interaction detection and model-checking performance on the same sensitivity slices.

The atlas does not estimate how often link misspecification occurs in psychological research. It does not cover every plausible outcome family, link, random-effects structure, measurement model, or predictor distribution. It also does not turn model diagnostics into a decision rule for the scientifically correct scale. Its role is narrower: to show how the mechanisms developed in the paper change across a declared set of nearby scenarios.

```{r}
)
```
